TargetRLF1: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), also known as sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), are infections that are typically spread through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex. These infections can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites, and they can have serious health consequences if left untreated. Common STIs include chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, human papillomavirus (HPV), and HIV/AIDS ayo Here are some ways to prevent the transmission of STIs:  Abstinence: The most effective way to prevent STIs is to abstain from sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral) with a partner who has an STI or whose STI status is unknown.  Use Condoms: Consistently and correctly using condoms during sexual activity can significantly reduce the risk of STI transmission. Use latex or polyurethane condoms for vaginal or anal sex, and use condoms or dental dams for oral sex.  Limit Sexual Partners: Having fewer sexual partners reduces your risk of exposure to STIs. Mutual monogamy with a partner who has tested negative for STIs can also lower your risk.  Communication: Talk openly and honestly with your sexual partners about STIs, testing, and safer sex practices. Encourage each other to get tested regularly for STIs.  Get Tested: Get tested for STIs regularly, especially if you are sexually active with multiple partners or have had unprotected sex. Many STIs do not cause symptoms, so testing is the only way to know your STI status.  Vaccination: Vaccines are available to prevent certain STIs, such as HPV and hepatitis B. Talk to your healthcare provider about whether vaccination is appropriate for you.  Avoid Sharing Needles: If you use injectable drugs, never share needles or other drug paraphernalia. Sharing needles can transmit STIs such as HIV and hepatitis B and C.  Practice Safer Sex: Avoid high-risk sexual behaviors, such as unprotected sex with multiple partners or engaging in sex while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Use your best judgment and prioritize your health and safety.  Routine Health Care: Attend regular check-ups with your healthcare provider for sexual health screenings and preventive care. Seek medical attention promptly if you experience symptoms of an STI or have been exposed to an STI.  By practicing safer sex, getting tested regularly, and communicating openly with your sexual partners, you can reduce your risk of contracting STIs and protect your sexual health. If you have questions or concerns about STI prevention, don't hesitate to speak with a healthcare provider or sexual health professional for guidance and support.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is a zoonosis – an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who'd died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream. Chimpanzees avoid humans wherever possible, so it is likely that SIVcpz crossed into humans as a result of human encroachment into forest areas. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s. It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of rare cases of pneumonia, cancer and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s.

It is important that you take all of the medicine your healthcare provider gives you because untreated or improperly treated Chlamydia can lead to serious complications. Do not share medicine for chlamydia with anyone. Recommended drugs include Doxycylcine, Azithromycin, Levofloxacin and Amoxicillin. TargetRLF1: Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as Herpes is caused by two types of herpes simplex virus. The genital infection caused by these two viruses manifests in the same way. Type 1 (HSV-1) mostly spreads by oral contact and causes infections in or around the mouth (oral herpes or cold sores). In rare circumstances, herpes (HSV-1 and HSV-2) can be transmitted from mother to child during delivery, causing neonatal herpes.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

TargetRLF1: The only way to completely avoid STIs is to not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. Also, the skin can release the virus (shed) from areas that do not have a visible herpes sore. For these reasons, condoms may not fully protect you from getting herpes. If your sex partner(s) has/have genital herpes, you can lower your risk of getting it if:•        Your partner takes an anti-herpes medicine every day. This is something your partner should discuss with his or her healthcare provider.•        You avoid having vaginal, anal, or oral sex when your partner has herpes symptoms (i.e., during an "outbreak").If you are pregnant and have genital herpes, prenatal care visits are very important. Some research suggest that a genital herpes infection may lead to miscarriage or make it more likely to deliver your baby too early. You can pass herpes to your unborn child before birth, but it more commonly passes during delivery. This can lead to a deadly infection in your baby (called neonatal herpes). It is important that you avoid getting genital herpes during pregnancy. Tell your healthcare provider if you have ever had a genital herpes diagnosis or symptoms. Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: Most people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes have no symptoms or only mild symptoms. Soem people people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected, but many people aren’t aware they have the infection and can pass along the virus to others without knowing. Symptoms can include painful, recurring blisters or ulcers. New infections may cause fever, body aches and swollen lymph nodes. Symptoms may be different during the first episode (or ‘outbreak’) of infection than during a recurrent episode. If symptoms occur, they often begin with tingling, itching or burning near where the sores will appear. Common genital herpes symptoms include bumps, blisters, or open sores (ulcers) around the genitals or anus. These sores and blisters are typically painful. Blisters may break open, ooze and then crust over. During their first infection, people may experience: •        fever•        body aches, joint pains•        sore throat (oral herpes)•        headache•        swollen lymph nodes near the infection. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathingshort periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. Herpes simplex infections in babies can be divided into three categories:localized skin infection— small, fluid-filled blisters on the skin and around the eyes and mouth that burst, crust over, and healencephalitis —an inflammation of the brain, which can cause problems with brain and spinal cord function, including seizuresdisseminated herpes infection— the most dangerous type of herpes infection. The herpes virus is spread throughout your child’s body and can affect multiple organs, including the liver, brain, lungs, and kidney.A baby infected with herpes may not have all the symptoms of the disease.Most symptoms surface by the end of the baby's first week, while more severe central nervous system problems will not appear until the baby's second week.If left untreated, encephalitis and disseminated herpes infections are potentially fatal.People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: Genital herpes or Herpes simplex virus (HSV), known as herpes, is a common infection that can cause painful blisters or ulcers. It primarily spreads by skin-to-skin contact. It is treatable but not curable. There are two types of herpes simplex virus. Type 1 (HSV-1) mostly spreads by oral contact and causes infections in or around the mouth (oral herpes or cold sores). It can also cause genital herpes. Most adults are infected with HSV-1. Type 2 (HSV-2) spreads by sexual contact and causes genital herpes. Most people have no symptoms or only mild symptoms. The infection can cause painful blisters or ulcers that can recur over time. Medicines can reduce symptoms but can’t cure the infection.Recurrent symptoms of both oral and genital herpes may be distressing. Genital herpes may also be stigmatizing and have an impact on sexual relationships. However, in time, most people with either kind of herpes adjust to living with the infection.

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of rare cases of pneumonia, cancer and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia infections also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infections spread through sexual contact, when vaginal fluid or semen containing the bacteria that causes chlamydia travels from one person to another. Sexual contact includes all kinds of sex, including sex that doesn’t involve penetration or ejaculation. There are lots of ways that the fluids from one person’s genitals can transmit the bacteria that causes chlamydia. Intercourse; bacteria pass from one person’s penis to their partner’s vagina or vice versa. Anal sex; bacteria pass from one person’s penis to their partner’s anus or vice versa. Sex involving toys; bacteria pass from a toy to a person’s mouth, penis, vagina or anus or through sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used. Oral sex; bacteria pass from one person’s mouth to their partner’s penis, vagina or anus, or vice versa. Manual stimulation of the genitals or anus; less commonly, infected vaginal fluid or semen can come in contact with a person’s eye, causing an infection called conjunctivitis (pink eye). For example, this can happen if you touch the genitals of an infected person and then rub your eyes without washing your hands first. A pregnant person with chlamydia can give the infection to their baby during childbirth and that can cause a type of eye infection in the baby which can damage their sight.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is a zoonosis – an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who'd died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream. Chimpanzees avoid humans wherever possible, so it is likely that SIVcpz crossed into humans as a result of human encroachment into forest areas. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s. It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of rare cases of pneumonia, cancer and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

Aqueous benzyl penicillin or procaine penicillin is recommended in infants with confirmed congenital syphilis or infants who are clinically healthy but whose mothers had untreated syphilis, inadequately treated syphilis (including treatment within 30 days of delivery), or syphilis treated with non-penicillin regimens. TargetRLF1: Chlamydia infections also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infections spread through sexual contact, when vaginal fluid or semen containing the bacteria that causes chlamydia travels from one person to another. Sexual contact includes all kinds of sex, including sex that doesn’t involve penetration or ejaculation. There are lots of ways that the fluids from one person’s genitals can transmit the bacteria that causes chlamydia. Intercourse; bacteria pass from one person’s penis to their partner’s vagina or vice versa. Anal sex; bacteria pass from one person’s penis to their partner’s anus or vice versa. Sex involving toys; bacteria pass from a toy to a person’s mouth, penis, vagina or anus or through sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used. Oral sex; bacteria pass from one person’s mouth to their partner’s penis, vagina or anus, or vice versa. Manual stimulation of the genitals or anus; less commonly, infected vaginal fluid or semen can come in contact with a person’s eye, causing an infection called conjunctivitis (pink eye). For example, this can happen if you touch the genitals of an infected person and then rub your eyes without washing your hands first. A pregnant person with chlamydia can give the infection to their baby during childbirth and that can cause a type of eye infection in the baby which can damage their sight.

TargetRLF1: Gonorrhea can be traced back to the earliest records of the human race. The Romans, Jews and Arabs all have documents referring to gonorrhea and each society had their own description of symptoms and treatment. The origins of Gonorrhea can be traced back to the Old Testament in the books of Leviticus and Genesis where it is described as a contagious, continuous emission of semen and painful erection. The disease has been referred to by various names in different societies. The Roman physician Galen in 130 AD described the disease as an "involuntary escape of semen".   Hippocrates (460–375 BC) called in "Strangury." The disease was also referred to as “The Clap,” referring either to the “clapping” sensation experienced by the infected person during urination or, as others believe, as a derivative of the French brothels, known as “Les Clapiers,” where the disease was quite rampant. In those days, men were considered victims and women as the source of the disease. The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications.. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Your need for testing depends on your personal risk for getting Chlamydia. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample. You should get tested regularly if you have unprotected sex with a new partner, multiple partners or a partner who has an STI. You should also get tested if you have symptoms or you are pregnant. Many people with Chlamydia don't have symptoms. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

TargetRLF1: Uncomplicated Chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection can be easily cured with antibiotics and is usually resolved within days or weeks. It is important that you take all of the medicine your healthcare provider gives you because untreated or improperly treated Chlamydia can lead to serious complications. Do not share medicine for chlamydia with anyone. Recommended drugs include Doxycylcine, Azithromycin, Levofloxacin and Amoxicillin. Although medicine will stop the infection, it will not undo any permanent damage caused by the disease. You should notify your sexual partner(s) to get tested and treated, if necessary. If the mother had a documented chlamydial infection during pregnancy that was untreated, presumptively treat the infant, even without confirmation of infection.
